diagnostic_evidence.quote: the unique entries of $R_k$ in its first column, are evaluated using this corresponding column of $W\Tilde{A}$ i.e. $R_k\hat e_1 = (D^k)^{-1}(W\Tilde{A})^{(k)}$

Thus arranging the cycles of matrix $A$ into columns of $\Tilde{A}$ and applying Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on its columns i.e. $W\Tilde{A}$ provides us all the circulant components of the matrix in only $\mathcal{O}(n^2 \log n)$ arithmetic operations.

issues.failure_explanation: Under the paper's own conventions (cycles as columns of $\tilde A$, i.e. $\tilde A(p,j)=A(p,(p-j)\bmod n)$ per the appendix example, and $W(p,q)=n^{-1/2}e^{-2\pi ipq/n}$), one computes $(W\tilde A)_{ij}=\sqrt{n}\,r_{j,i}\omega^{-ij}$, where $(r_{p,k})_p$ is the first column of $R_k$. Hence the first column of $R_k$ equals $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}D^k(\text{row }k\text{ of }W\tilde A)^T$. Step 4 instead returns $(D^k)^{-1}(\text{column }k\text{ of }W\tilde A)$, the wrong slice with wrong phases and missing normalization. Concrete 2x2 counterexample: for $A=[[a_{00},a_{01}],[a_{10},a_{11}]]$ the true first column of $R_1$ is $((a_{00}-a_{11})/2,(a_{10}-a_{01})/2)^T$, while Step 4 gives $(D^1)^{-1}(W\tilde A)^{(1)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(a_{01}+a_{10},a_{10}-a_{01})^T$ (e.g. $a_{00}=1$, others $0$: $(1/2,0)$ vs $(0,0)$). The prose formula repeats the same error; '$\hat e_1$' should be $\hat e_0$ under the paper's 0-indexing, and Step 3 assigns $L[j]\gets\Lambda_j$ although the cycles $\Lambda_j$ are never computed from the input $A$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct Step 4 (and the identical prose formula) to: first column of $R_k$ = $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}D^k(\text{row }k\text{ of }W\tilde A)^T$ under the stated conventions (or the equivalent conjugate-FFT form), including normalization, and make the construction of $\tilde A$ and $\Lambda_j$ explicit steps.
issues.overall_effect: The circulant components produced by the algorithm as literally specified are incorrect, so the block's output contract fails for any verbatim implementation. The decomposition method, its $O(n^2\log n)$ cost, and the downstream CD multiplication remain valid once the formula is corrected.
issues.title: Circulant decomposition FFT step returns wrong components (wrong slice and phase of W tilde-A)
issues.why_classification: A one-line local formula correction (slice, phase direction, normalization) restores the algorithm; the method, complexity claims, and all downstream results survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: W\bm l_k \circ W(D^k\bm b) = W \bm l_k \circ WD^kW^{*}W\bm b =  W \bm l_k \circ C^kW\bm b

issues.failure_explanation: The correct Fourier identity is $W(R_tD^tB)=(WR_tW^*)(WD^tW^*)WB=\mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda_t)C^tWB$, where $\hat\lambda_t$ is the eigenvalue vector of the circulant $R_t$ (the DFT of its first column $R_A[t]$). Step 5 uses $L_A[t]$ as this diagonal, but per the decomposition algorithm's output '$L[j]\gets\Lambda_j$' stores the cycles, and cycle entries differ from circulant eigenvalues (2x2 example: $\Lambda_0=(a_{00},a_{11})$ while the eigenvalues of $R_0$ are $((a_{00}+a_{11}+a_{01}+a_{10})/2,(a_{00}+a_{11}-a_{01}-a_{10})/2)$; with $B=I$ the algorithm returns $W^*\Lambda_0W\ne R_0$). The second line is also not a valid transform of $\Delta A R_{B_t}D^t=W^*[(W\Delta AW^*)\mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda_{B_t})C^tW]$: as written, $(\mathrm{FFT}(\Delta A)L_B[t])C^t$ omits the conjugating $W^*$ on $\Delta A$ and the trailing $W$, besides using $\Lambda$ instead of $\hat\lambda$. As specified, Step 5 computes neither $\tilde AB$ nor $\Delta A\tilde B$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Rewrite Step 5 with the correct identities: $\tilde AB = W^*(\sum_t \mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda_t)C^tWB)$ with $\hat\lambda_t$ the DFT of the stored first column $R_A[t]$ (not the cycle $\Lambda_t$), and $\Delta A\tilde B = W^*(\sum_t (W\Delta AW^*)\mathrm{diag}(\hat\lambda_{B_t})C^tW)$.
issues.overall_effect: The algorithm's core computation (Step 5) does not produce the first-order approximation of eq:first_order_expansion that the algorithm promises; the returned output is wrong as written. The method, its $O(n^2\log n)$ complexity claim, and the accuracy claims are recoverable by local corrections.
issues.title: CD multiplication Step 5 uses cycles instead of circulant eigenvalues and omits required conjugations
issues.why_classification: A local rewrite of Step 5's two formula lines (correct diagonals and conjugations) restores the algorithm; no claim, guarantee, or complexity bound is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We can rewrite the product \( AB \) as \( A W^* W B \).

issues.failure_explanation: Steps 1-2 define $\tilde A=AW^*$ and $\tilde B=WB$ with the paper's unitary $W$, so $\tilde A\tilde B=A(W^*W)B=AB$ exactly, and the paper's own displayed first-order formula (and the identity $AB=F^*(A)\cdot F(B)$) carries no scaling factor. Step 7 nevertheless returns $M=\frac{1}{n}(\tilde A_{approx}\tilde B+\Delta A\tilde B_{approx})$, which under the stated unitary convention equals $(AB-\Delta A\,\Delta\tilde B)/n$, i.e. approximately $AB/n$ — a factor-$n$ error. The $1/n$ would only be correct for unnormalized DFT conventions, which contradict the $W$ used in Steps 1-2 and the displayed identities.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Delete the $1/n$ factor in Step 7 (or, if unnormalized FFTs are intended, redefine Steps 1-2 to use the unnormalized transforms and adjust the displayed identity $AB=F^*(A)\cdot F(B)$ accordingly).
issues.overall_effect: Under the paper's stated (unitary) conventions the algorithm's output is scaled by $1/n$, so its stated contract (approximation of $AB$) fails, and the algorithm is mutually inconsistent with the paper's displayed formula. The sparsification method itself is unaffected once the normalization is fixed.
issues.title: FFT-sparsification multiplication scales its output by 1/n under the paper's unitary W
issues.why_classification: Removing (or consistently redefining) the single $1/n$ factor restores the algorithm's output contract; nothing else in the method or its guarantees changes.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof applies Theorem elizabeths to $F=-f$ with the Lipschitz constant $L=2\|D_1\|_F^2\|D_2\|_2^2$, which yields $P[f\le Ef-t]\le\exp(-(n-2)t^2/(24L^2))=\exp(-(n-2)t^2/(96\|D_1\|_F^4\|D_2\|_2^4))$ — exactly the bound derived and labeled in the proof. The corollary's statement claims the same bound with 48 in the denominator, a factor of 2 stronger than anything established; no sharper Lipschitz constant is derived anywhere (the symmetric minimum only enters $L$, not the $24L^2$ structure).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 48 by 96 in the corollary's statement to match the proof, or derive and use a Lipschitz constant smaller by $\sqrt{2}$ to justify 48.
issues.overall_effect: The constant in the corollary's stated bound is unsupported; the qualitative concentration conclusion (relevant when $L^2/n\to 0$) and its downstream qualitative uses are unaffected.
issues.title: Concentration corollary claims constant 48; its proof derives 96
issues.why_classification: Changing one constant to match the derivation is a routine local fix; the concentration statement and all its uses survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where for each $n_i$, $\mathbb{G}_{n_i}$ is one of $\mathbb{SO}(n_i)$, $\mathbb{SO}^{-}(n_i)$, $\mathbb{SU}(n_i)$, $\mathbb{U}(n_i)$, or $\mathbb{Sp}(2n_i)$.
Let $A = Q_1 D_1 Q_2$ and $B = Q_3 D_2 Q_4$ be singular value decompositions of $A$ and $B$, and $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$ be Haar distributed unitary matrices.

issues.failure_explanation: The corollary's proof invokes the quoted concentration theorem with $X=\mathbf{O}(n)$, but the theorem as stated in the source admits only $\mathbb{SO}(n)$, $\mathbb{SO}^{-}(n)$, $\mathbb{SU}(n)$, $\mathbb{U}(n)$, or $\mathbb{Sp}(2n)$ as factors — $O(n)$ is not among them. The exclusion is substantive: $O(n)$ has two connected components at Hilbert-Schmidt distance 2, and an $L$-Lipschitz function that is 0 on $SO(n)$ and $2L$ on $SO^{-}(n)$ has $P[F\ge EF+t]=1/2$ for $t\le L$, violating the stated $\exp(-(n-2)t^2/24L^2)$ bound, so the theorem does not extend verbatim to $O(n)$. The corollary's conclusion does hold for this particular $f$ (since $f(RQ)=f(Q)$ for a signature-flip $R$), but that reduction is absent from the source. The setting is also inconsistent with Lemma th:expected_norm_square, which assumes Haar unitary (complex) matrices while the Lipschitz computation uses the real transpose $Q^T$.

failure_location.quote: Let us apply the Theorem \ref{elizabeths}, with $X = \mathbf{O}(n)$ the norm $\norm{\cdot}_F$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Apply the theorem on $SO(n)$ (or $U(n)$ in the complex setting) and add the observation that $f(RQ)=f(Q)$ for a signature-flip $R$, so the law of $f$ on $O(n)$ coincides with its law on $SO(n)$; or cite a version of the concentration theorem that covers $O(n)$.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary's derivation is formally invalid as written (theorem used outside its stated hypotheses); its conclusion requires an additional short argument not present in the source. Downstream qualitative uses are unaffected in substance.
issues.title: Concentration theorem invoked on O(n), outside its quoted hypotheses
issues.why_classification: A short standard argument (restrict to one component and use the sign-flip symmetry of $f$) repairs the invocation; the corollary's conclusion and its uses survive unchanged.

issues.failure_explanation: The statement asserts the exact identity $\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|_F]=\frac34\|A\|_F\|B\|_F$, whose right-hand side is random unless the norms are conditioned on. The proof computes only unconditional second moments, $\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|_F^2]=mpn\frac{a^4}{9}+mpn(n-1)\frac{a^4}{16}$, and shows the ratio $\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|^2]/(\mathbf{E}[\|A\|^2]\mathbf{E}[\|B\|^2])=(9n+7)/(16n)\approx 9/16$ only for $n\gg 1$. The final step — 'When $\|A\|_F,\|B\|_F$ are known quantities, $\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|_F]\approx\frac34\|A\|_F\|B\|_F$' — is a non sequitur: the conditioning on the norms is never handled, $\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|_F]$ is silently replaced by $\sqrt{\mathbf{E}[\|AB\|_F^2]}$ without a concentration argument, and an asymptotic approximate second-moment relation is converted into an exact first-moment identity. The exact claim is false in small dimensions: for $n=1$ the second-moment ratio is $1$, not $9/16$, and $\mathbf{E}[AB]=a^2/4\ne(3/4)AB$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken the statement to an asymptotic approximation — for $n\to\infty$, $\|AB\|_F/(\|A\|_F\|B\|_F)\to 3/4$ in expectation and probability for i.i.d. $U(0,a)$ entries — proved via a concentration argument for $\|AB\|_F$ plus norm concentration to handle the conditioning, dropping the exact identity and the 'known quantities' formulation.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem's exact first-moment identity is unsupported and ill-posed as stated (random right-hand side, unjustified conditioning); the $3/4$ factor used as the Case-2 denominator in Proposition th:estimated_relative_error rests on this unsupported derivation.
issues.title: Uniform-entry norm theorem asserts an exact identity its proof does not establish
issues.why_classification: The exact identity must be weakened to an asymptotic, concentration-based statement and the conditioning step justified — a contained nontrivial argument with a limited weakening; a recognizably comparable result (the $3/4$ factor for large $n$) survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: While the expectation $\mathbf{E}[\norm{\Delta A .\Delta B}_F]$ in the numerator can be approximated by that of a normal distribution as the entries of the residue matrices are equally likely to be of either signs
where $c \approx 1$ are constants for a given type of matrices.

It is significant that the expected errors can be evaluated a priori using $
orm{\Delta A}_F$, $
orm{\Delta B}$, $
orm{A}_F$, and $
orm{B}$ in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ arithmetic operations before the approximate multiplication (see \cref{th:estimated_relative_error}).

issues.failure_explanation: Neither case estimate is actually established. (i) The claimed variance decay of $\|AB\|_F$ and $\|\Delta A.\Delta B\|_F$ is asserted, citing th:concentrationprob 'for example' — but that corollary concerns Haar conjugations of fixed diagonal matrices and says nothing about residues of truncated decompositions or their product. (ii) The replacement $\mathbf{E}[X/Y]\approx\mathbf{E}[X]/\mathbf{E}[Y]$ requires control of the denominator's fluctuations and lower tail, not merely variance decay. (iii) The numerator's normal approximation assumes residue entries are 'equally likely to be of either signs' — unproved, and false as an i.i.d. model since CD/SVD residues are deterministic functions of $A$ and $B$. (iv) The constants $c$ are unspecified. The two-case conclusion is thus a chain of heuristics presented as a proved proposition, and the results section leans on it for the a priori error-evaluation capability.

failure_location.quote: We know that $Var[\norm{AB}_F]$ and $Var[\norm{\Delta A.\Delta B}_F]$ $\to 0$ for large $n$ and a random distribution of the entries (as in \cref{th:concentrationprob}, for example).

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either demote the proposition to an explicitly labeled heuristic estimate, or prove it under explicit hypotheses (e.g., i.i.d. entry models for $A$, $B$ and their residues) via second-moment computations plus concentration bounds controlling the variance of both norms and the lower tail of $\|AB\|_F$, with explicit constants $c$.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's central a priori error estimates (both cases of the proposition) are unestablished by the given proof; the prose claims that expected errors 'can be evaluated a priori' and scale as the product of the relative errors inherit this gap.
issues.title: A priori relative-error proposition proved only by unestablished heuristic steps
issues.why_classification: Making the proposition honest requires either a contained but genuinely nontrivial analysis (moment computations plus concentration under explicit hypotheses) or demotion to a heuristic; the claim's support changes, but no global proof architecture, advertised regime, or empirical result is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Now using the fact that for Haar distributed matrices we have $\mathbf{E}[|Q_{i,j}|^4]  = \frac{2}{n(n+1)}$ and $\mathbf{E}[|Q_{i,j}|^2 |Q_{k,l}|^2]  = \frac{1}{n(n+1)}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof of $\mathbf{E}[S^2]$ relies on the premise $\mathbf{E}[|Q_{i,j}|^2|Q_{k,l}|^2]=\frac{1}{n(n+1)}$ for all $(i,j)\ne(k,l)$. For Haar unitary matrices this holds only when $i=k$ or $j=l$; when both indices differ the correct value is $\frac{1}{n^2-1}$ (and for Haar orthogonal matrices the values differ again), so the necessary case split is missing and the stated formula is false. Counterexample: $D_1=D_2=I$ gives $S=\|Q\|_F^2=n$ deterministically, so $\mathbf{E}[S^2]=n^2$, whereas the lemma gives $n(n^2+1)/(n+1)$ ($n=2$: $10/3$ versus $4$). Lemma lem:added-2 inherits the error and yields a negative 'variance' in the same case, $\text{Var}(S)=n(1-n)/(n+1)<0$, and the subsequent displayed formulas for $\mathbf{E}[\sqrt{S}]$ are built on this false $\text{Var}(S)$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redo the fourth-moment computation with the correct Haar moments, splitting the cases $(i,j)=(k,l)$, exactly one index equal, and both indices different, and restate the formulas for $\mathbf{E}[S^2]$, $\text{Var}(S)$, and $\mathbf{E}[\sqrt{S}]$ accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: Lemmas lem:added-1 and lem:added-2 are false as stated (the latter can even return a negative variance), and the appendix's displayed estimates of $\mathbf{E}[\sqrt{S}]$ built on them are unreliable. No main-text result cites these lemmas, so the damage is confined to the appendix.
issues.title: False Haar fourth-moment premise makes the variance lemmas wrong
issues.why_classification: Both stated lemmas are false and must be replaced by corrected formulas via a contained but nontrivial recomputation of Haar fourth moments (Weingarten-type case split); no global architecture or main-text result is affected.
